utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Monday, and I greet the accused, the Defence counsels, the Prosecutor, and everyone helping us. Mr. Registrar, I believe you have some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's correct, we have a few IC numbers, as requested by the parties. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Zrinko Tokic. The IC numbers assigned will be as follows: The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC1066. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC1067. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC1068. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit IC1069. And we have a further document submitted by the Praljak Defence, and the document is the Praljak Defence reply to Prosecution objection to documents tendered through Slobodan Praljak, and that will be Exhibit IC1070. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Praljak Defence sent us a new schedule, and it seems that the witness Vlado Zeric [phoen] has been withdrawn, he will not be heard, which means that in the week of October 12, we will only be hearing witness Bragan Krsic [phoen]. I believe Ms. Alaburic had a few words for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was going to be me, but the particular point doesn't arise, so we needn't take the Chamber's time at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring in the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vlado Sakic. I was born on the 2nd of September, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a university professor and a scholar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you already testified in court regarding the events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never testified. Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, just a few -- just some information so that this hearing runs smoothly. You will be answering questions put to you by the Defence team of General Praljak, and two hours have been allocated for this phase. After this, the other Defence counsel will have one hour altogether to put questions to you, if they deem it useful, and then the Prosecutor, who's on your right, will have two hours for his cross-examination. The three Judges on the Bench -- normally there's four of us, but one of us is ill. But the three Judges on the Bench will also ask questions, if need be. You're a scholar, you're a teacher, you are a faculty teacher, so you know that your answers must be very specific, brief, and to the point. Please refrain from going astray. If you do not understand a question, ask the person putting the question to reformulate it. We have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half. Unfortunately, we started a bit late, but it's -- we're not to blame, but we will have our first break in about an hour and 25 minutes. You made the solemn declaration, you took an oath, so you're now a witness for justice, and for the days to come you will no longer contact the Defence team of General Praljak. That's all I had to say, and I will now give the floor to Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, expert witness. Good afternoon to everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to say, to save time, a couple of minutes of this witness's testimony -- well, I'd like to ask for the usher's assistance so that we can place on the ELMO the witness's curriculum vitae, and I'd like my learned friend of the Prosecution to agree to having everything down on paper. This is what it looks like, Mr. Scott, this document, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I'm being asked to agree to, Your Honour. We look at documents every day in the courtroom. I'm not sure how this is different than any other day, so I'm not being difficult, I just -- I don't understand what counsel is requesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I haven't requested anything yet, just a little patience. I just wanted to first check to see whether you had the document, and then I'll go on and ask what I want. So this is a summary of the curriculum vitae, setting out the witness's professional life. He's from the Ivo Pilar Institute, and with your permission and with the permission of my learned friend of the Prosecution, I would like to ask leading questions about the CV, and I think we'll be able to get through it quicker. Of course, we provided a copy of the CV to everyone. This is just a summary of the CV that we have otherwise provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have before you the document. And could the usher place it on the overhead projector, please. Is it there? You have it on the screen. Right, fine. So take a look at it now, please. And I have briefly extracted the main points from your curriculum vitae, so I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions, and it might need some explanation. Under number 1, personal data, just confirm, please, whether all that data is correct.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that data there is correct. Thank you. Now, under point 2, the first section of point 2 relates to some of your earlier activities, various earlier activities. Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, once again, staying with number 2, the second section under the title "Currently" or -- that has a number of points. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, apparently you've been a UN expert regarding criminal matters. Could you tell us what exactly this means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't an expert in criminal law. What I was was a recognised UN expert, which is a status a little lower than a UN expert, and I was granted that status during 1989-1990, when I was invited by the Helsinki Institute of the United Nations to be a scholarship-holder, and then I was invited to attend the 8th Congress of the United Nations as a recognised expert, as it's called - that's the term used - which was held on Cuba. And it had to do with the prevention of crime and conduct with transgressors. And it is within the frameworks of the Economic Council of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to turn the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have a look at that next page, section 3, Roman III. Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let's move on to section IV. If you've looked through it, just tell us, please, whether all that is correct.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are general statements, all of them correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now I have a question to ask with respect to that third point, "Board of editors," and specifically -- just let me finish. In your binder, during the proofing session, you were given 3D03523, which is a book entitled "Military Psychology," but tell me -- and I see here and you said that you were on the editorial board. Do you remember that book for any specific reason?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I do. But before I tell you, Counsel, can I put right something in section III? It says here that I was the ex-president of the Croatian Penological Association, and the vice-president as well. That's not correct. I was the president of the Croatian Penological Association of Croatia and the vice-president of the Croatian Psychological Society, so I held high-ranking positions in two associations. And now to tell you about the book "Military Psychology." "Military Psychology" otherwise is a textbook, and I was on the board of editors, and this book was first -- the idea about it was started by the Psychological Department within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and it rallied together a large number of psychologists who wrote a three-part book, textbook, three volumes, and it was accepted as a textbook at all the -- for all the Croatian universities. Now, it is particularly interesting to note, in this regard, that the book has been translated into Hungarian and that I, personally, like all the editors of the individual chapters and the editor-in-chief, received a review by a well-known Hungarian university professor and well-known psychologist who -- well, he made a high assessment -- he gave high praise for the book, and he sent this review to a large number of European countries with the recommendation that this textbook, written on the basis of the Croatian war of independence, or the war in the former Yugoslavia, that it was an excellent textbook and that he highly recommended it in Europe, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in section IV, we see there listed one of your activities, the promotion and popularisation of social science there, and there was a project that was called "Scientific Thursday," with many guest speakers. I just mentioned a few of them, and they're listed here. And I have two questions about that, Doctor. What was the aim or, rather, what was the importance of this project, "Scientific Thursday," and do you perhaps remember any other well-known names? Or I can ask you about them. For instance, at that "Scientific Thursday," did you have Mr. Martin Bell, a British MP and well-known British journalist as a guest speaker? Did he attend?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but may I give an explanation here? This "Scientific Thursday" project was an open, public forum for popularising science, the social sciences. I was director of the institute, and I chaired that whole event, and it took place when the aggression against Croatia was at its peak. And we tried, in that way, as scholars, to internationalise the events that were taking place, and that is why we invited well-known individuals to be guest speakers, as Alain Finkielkraut, there was Dr. Peter Kampits, an Austrian, Mr. Martin Bell, and I remember Janos Bugajski was there as well, so a series of well-known names in the field; journalists, publicists, cultural figures who dealt with these conflicts. Our last guest speaker a year ago was Jacques Klein, who came, invited by the institution for the ceremony of the peaceful reintegration of Vukovar. He came at my personal invitation for the 10th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Mr. Jacques Klein. You mean Ambassador Jacques Klein, who was a UN envoy with regard to the integration of Southern Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In East Slavonia, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So all that is correct, all the rest of it under section IV?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now we come to section V, where I list some of the basic characteristics of the social institute. We have already seen that you were the director of the institute, the Ivo Pilar Institute, and I have listed some other facts there. Just tell me if everything there is correct about the institute.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Everything is correct. There is more to be added, but this is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course there is more, but we would need more time to talk about everything. I would like to ask you just one thing in this regard. When I was reading about the institute and when I spoke to you, and when I learned that a lot of importance is given to the multidisciplinary approach to science in your projects, or, rather, multidisciplinary method, could you please tell us why do you think that this is an important fact, in comparison with a traditional specialist approach to various projects? But please be brief.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: We founded the institute in early -- in the early 1990s, when Croatia became an independent and democratic state, and our main motto was through research to facts. You have to understand the political and social background that Croatia had before that, and if you do, then you will understand the motto. We immediately opted for a multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approach because we followed the logic of similar institutions in the West. We wanted to adopt their approach. We wanted to be organised in the same way in our research. For example, my idols were Gallup and the National Opinion Research Centre, a large institute, the Chicago University, and in Germany Max Planck Institute in the communist and the former communist area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and a few more questions just to round off the topic. You have been in enrolled in various projects. Could you please tell me, as a scientist, what would you say that is the focus of your scientific and scholarly interest? What is your main topic? What is your main point of interest?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I've been involved in scientific research for 30 years now. I've had several areas of interest that I have been involved in, but in general terms, all these areas have to do with the backbone of my scientific and teaching activity, and that's social psychology. Within that general area, my special areas of interest are social psychology of immigration, social psychology of crime, penological psychology. I've also dealt with social psychology of violence, of war, and so on and so forth. This was my main point of interest in the early 1990s. Now I am intensely involved in the research of social identity, which is one of the areas of social psychology that has been most extensively researched in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And now, please, Professor, let's bring this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you know about my role as a watch-dog for the interpreters, so therefore I would like to ask you and, of course, Professor Sakic, that you have to try to slow down and to wait until the translation is ended on both sides, and to start with your answers, Professor, only when the interpreters will finish their own translation. So I hope that you will be doing this and to comply with this request. If I take the floor now, I would also like you -- to ask you, Professor, about one particular small fact and issue. You mentioned that your book and activities had also been discussed and supported by one of the Hungarian professors of sociology, and since I'm Hungarian, I would only like to ask you about the name of that particular professor, if you still remember it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say, unfortunately, that at this moment I can't remember his name, but I can look it up and I can tell you tomorrow. I don't remember. I have not expected such a question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, it is not so urgent and not so important, but I would also appreciate if you will find it out. Thank you. And, Mr. Kovacic, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it and I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have submitted to the Court document 03721, which is a 3D document, and that is your expert report. Everybody has it, everybody has seen it, everybody has had plenty of time to read it. Let me just ask you whether this is your work. Did you draft this expert report?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I drafted it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to bring this to an end, could you please tell us, in a couple of sentences, as a citizen of the Republic of Croatia, where you resided during the events in question from the 1990s onwards, to what extent were you personally familiar with what was going on in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: As for the events in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I learned about them just like any other citizen of Croatia, from the media, in conversations with friends and acquaintances, as well as other scholars and scientists that I cooperated with, and then in some other ways which were all public, which means that I didn't use any other ways, save for the normal ways that any citizen used, and also I was reading publications about Bosnia and Herzegovina that were being published all those years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, just a minute. Mr. Kovacic is no longer putting questions about your resume, but before looking into the crux of your report, I'd like to come back to your resume. I noted on number II, under number II, that you were a guest speaker at Notre Dame in Indiana, in the Chicago university Notre Dame, a Catholic university. In 2009, President Obama was also a guest speaker at Notre Dame, and actually made a speech at Notre Dame on dialogue and respect for freedom. So you were a guest speaker at this eminent university. Did you give a speech or a lecture, and if so, what was the topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not give a speech or a lecture. I was there to talk to a centre in Notre Dame that was dealing with the research of violence at the time and the establishment of peace. I was there to agree -- a possible cooperation between my institute and that particular centre, which means that I did not deliver a speech or a lecture at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Kovacic, and I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since your curriculum has already been submitted to the Trial Chamber, together with your expert report, and we have dealt with only a few excerpts - the number under which this was submitted is 3D03727 - I don't have any more questions about the professor's CV. I believe that you've got the impression. I would like to move to the essence, and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow Mr. Praljak to put questions to the witness because he is the best suited to put questions to the witness because he has been educated in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, General Praljak. Professor, I have a question. I'm trying to understand how this Ivo Pilar Institute works. As far as the budget is concerned, could you tell us whether this institute is financed directly by the government, whether there are donors, donations, or whether you make your own money? So could you please tell us whether it is an autonomous institution or whether it depends on government funds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the institute, Ivo Pilar, is funded in the same way as all the other institutes and public universities in Croatia are funded. This is a public scientific institute which is funded from the budget of the Ministry of Science and Education. In addition to that, we also rely on donations from Croatian and foreign foundations, and some of our financing comes from market-oriented projects commissioned by our buyers. Our buyers can be from the industry, from other social institutes, from political institutions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question on this topic. Could you tell us whether the head of this institute is appointed by the government or whether he is elected by a panel of scholars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the head is appointed by the management board, and the management board is composed of scientists and scholars. And the head is appointed based on the opinion of the scientific board, and then the management board selects the head based on that opinion. The Ministry of Science is in charge of supervising the appointment procedure. It does not meddle with the autonomy of the institute's scientific work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examination by Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Sakic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Two things. First of all, time is very precious and short at this Tribunal. We have a lot of work to do. We have a number of documents to go through primarily concerning social psychology. And the second thing is the interpretation. Please wait for my question to be over, and then I would kindly ask you for the shortest possible answers. What we are going to go through from the book that is filed under number 3D352 -- 3D3521, the book has been submitted and we can only go through some of the elements of the book because we don't have much more time. 3D03521. You have the book before --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but -- I'll wait for Judge Trechsel to find -- excuse me, Your Honour, and I apologise for the interruption, but I was under the impression that we were here to hear about the report that the Professor has written and submitted to the Prosecution and to the Chamber, and we would be here to talk about his report and not about some book that is not his report, so I -- unless this is just a passing reference to a particular citation, that's one thing, but I just heard Mr. Praljak say that he intends to spend his entire time going through this book, and I think that's beyond the scope of this exercise and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, could you please explain? What is the relevance of the book in relation to the expert? Is the book mentioned as a footnote in the expert report? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the book, in several places you can find a number of experiments which, in a classical textbook of social psychology, a textbook that has had several reprints, which talk about all of the elements based on which the expert has drafted his report and has reached some conclusions. The experiments are mentioned in there, as well as some other things, and in order for anybody to understand the essence of the matter, we have to go through the main parts which concern the behaviour of an individual in extreme circumstances, which, of course, war is one of them. And this is simply -- I don't think that we need to repeat what has been written in the expert report, because everybody can read it, but it is necessary to clarify some other things, which are based in science and proved by experiments, in order to gain an insight and properly understand the behaviour of a certain number of individuals during a war or faced with some other extreme situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, let me remind you that you have two hours for your cross-examination, so if you stand up every time to raise objections, we're going to spend the entire time on objections, whilst it would be more interesting to see the contents of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. We should see the contents of the report and not a book that is not the report. And this is not counting against my time, and that's never been the practice, and I'm sure it's not now. I do object, Your Honour, and if I think there's a proper objection, I will make it. The Prosecution has been very brief in the use of time in this courtroom. We have -- we use less time than anybody else, so I won't be overly sensitive about my use of time. Your Honour, I do object to this procedure. The specific procedure under the Rules is that a report is prepared, it's submitted to the Chamber and to the Prosecution, and to the co-accused, for that matter, so that specific preparations can be made by the Chamber and by the parties to deal with that report, not something else. This is different than another witness. A specific report is prepared, it is made available, and that is what we should be covering. With no offence intended to the witness, if the report doesn't speak for itself, if the witness has not prepared his report so that anyone can understand his report within the four corners of his report, well, with due respect to the witness, that's a problem for him: We are here to receive this report, not something else, and I do object to spending the time going through a book that is not part of this report. And Mr. Praljak, at least in the translation, said before, and I'm looking at it again - I have it on the screen: "What we are going to do is go through the book." We are going to go through the book, which is not his report, and we do object to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have an expert witness in front of us. His report deals with two main themes, the history as the main thread for the development in Bosnia and Herzegovina and then the concept of social identity and stabilisation of identity, and then the birth -- the rising of nationalism. And then we have a second chapter, a predictable conflict, various approaches, and then the responsibility of the international community. So this is the extent of his report. You have just alluded to a book. Now, where does that book fit in the expert's report? You could have asked first whether he studied the book before writing his report, and what was the impact of reading the book, because otherwise Mr. Scott is right, we're going to spend time on a book whilst we're here and we're supposed to be looking at an expert report. I spent several hours reading it, and I haven't read the book. If you told me that you were going to put questions about the book, I would have read it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, this isn't a book, it's a textbook. That's the difference. A textbook on physics deals with the laws of gravitation. And when the expert mentions conformism, belonging to a group, outside a group, when he mentions elements of fear, then that is a textbook which sets forth the elements of knowledge about social psychology. It's not a book by an author recounting a tale from his own perspective. These are experiments -- or, rather, a textbook that speaks about overall knowledge in social psychology and experiments and so on. And when the expert in the book says that an object in a room, a badminton racquet or whatever, can change a feeling of aggression, then that is in a textbook. So it's not a book; it's a textbook. And a math textbook or a physics textbook, in those kinds of books, you repeat all the knowledge in a particular branch, in a certain section, whether it's analytical geometry or Newton's physics. So without these elements that we need to mention here, they form the essence -- the substance, of course, with two or three other chapters mentioned by the expert, historical reasons and so on, the definition of a nation, a state, and so on. Now, unfortunately, I can't go through all that in the space of two hours, but that's why I elected to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, do put your questions, but let me remind you that the three Judges have read your report. They've all spent time reading your report. So if we are of the opinion that you get outside of the scope of the report, we'll stop you. Is this understood? You have the floor, you may put your questions, but keep in mind, please, that the Judges have read the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, in the procedural sense can I respond to the objection raised by my learned friend Mr. Scott? And I have in mind, first of all, Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The expert finding has been filed. It was filed on time. Everybody received a copy, and the party, in this case the Defence, is authorised to seek to tender the expert report any time. Now, according to that same rule, the opposite party, that is to say, the Prosecution in this case, has the right to seek to ask that the witness come in for cross-examination, and nowhere in the Rule does it say that the Court will assess this request. It's an automatic process. So if the other side wants to hear the expert witness live and to cross-examine them, they put in a request and that is what they do, and that is what the Prosecution did. And they are able to cross-examine on the report, and the Defence need not -- it need not at all deal with the expert report. The expert report is a written document. The witness is an expert. We've established why he's an expert, and we've established that he stands by his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Kovacic, you know that the Judges are experienced and they know how this Tribunal works. I do not quite agree with what you've just said. If a party wants a report to be tendered into evidence, failing any opposition, the Trial Chamber -- I repeat -- under the Rules, a party asking a report to be tendered, well, if there's no objections by the other party, the report is tendered and the witness will not appear. You can see how things work in other Trial Chambers. But if a party challenges the report when it is sought to be tendered, which is the case here, and wants to cross-examine the witness, then the party is allowed to ask questions of the witness, but it is mainly the cross-examination that is the main purpose of the proceedings, and only then does the Trial Chamber decide to admit the report or not. So do not take for granted that report as being tendered. The Trial Chamber has not yet ruled on it. It will depend on your questions and on the cross-examination. It may happen that it's not going to be admitted. So, please, do not get me wrong and don't be mistaken. The Judges will assess the relevance of their questions based on this handbook on psychology, but at face value it doesn't seem to be relevant to me. But let's wait for General Praljak's questions. But if the Trial Chamber thinks that we're wasting our time, which is sometimes my feeling, we will put an end to it. Are we clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please carry on. I will listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't wish to take up any time. I just wanted to respond to the objection raised by my learned friend Mr. Scott, and that objection contained within it the assertion, and I go back to the transcript to see exactly what it contained -- he implied, in actual fact, that the Defence is duty-bound to examine on the matter of the report. Now, I agree, Your Honours, with what you just said and how you explained the Rules of Procedure. I agree with that 100 per cent, and that's the truth of it. The Prosecutor can examine the witness on his expert report for as long as he likes, and that is why the report is being placed on the table just as you said, and I'm only speaking about procedure now. And I'd like to say that in terms of content, Mr. Praljak did show the link because, in our humble opinion, that is the case. We can present it in the way in which we consider it to be methodologically correct to do so. It's up to us to weigh the situation up. But as the objection was raised, it is not based on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and is not in keeping with the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'd like to just respond ever so briefly. I couldn't disagree more with counsel on this point. Rule 94 bis (A) is quite clear. The reason why it says "the full statement and/or report of any expert witness to be called shall be disclosed," is so that that is the subject matter that is addressed by the witness. It isn't just for fun, it isn't just for leisure time that a particular report is prepared and submitted to the Judges and to the parties. It is so that evidence can be reviewed and prepared ahead of time. And if I may say so, this is bait and switch. This is prepare one set of written materials and give that to everyone, give that to the Judges, give that to the Prosecution, give that to the co-accused, and then come to court and talk about something else altogether, even if it's potentially somewhat related. This is simply, as Your Honour, said, Mr. President, completely contrary to Tribunal practice. Now, if it's one footnote -- if it's one footnote or something like that that's going to take a matter of a minute or two minute, I'll sit down and I won't get back up on it. But, again, what the clear indication has been, and Mr. Praljak has in fact confirmed that in his conversation over the last few minutes, says that he intends to spend his time on the book, and that this is not proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have taken due note of all this. You know that the Judges and everybody are interested, in the first place, in the expert's report. Now, if there's a connection between the book and the report, do show it, but -- because so far we don't know whether there's any connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: To add to what our President just said and repeated, the following: That we know we have had a number of cases when we discussed the possibility of having given the time to Mr. Praljak for asking questions. I would like to emphasise now that we have had a great numbers of weeks where Mr. Praljak, as a witness, himself, has been asked about issues and he answered to them. Now, as we always recall, the general rule is that the accused are represented by their counsel. Now I have the French text before me, the -- [Interpretation] "In exceptional circumstances and upon leave granted by the Trial Chamber, an accused can address a witness directly in order to put questions to them." [In English] And that is really that Mr. Praljak has to clarify now on which exceptional questions he would like to ask questions from the -- actually from the expert witness, and because you had several weeks here to express your own position, you have had a great number of documents which you have submitted, yourselves, and therefore I really believe that you have to recognise the limits which -- the limits of the rights which you have and not to continue and continuously asking questions which are not well founded. So it is why -- that's why I ask you to indicate, very briefly, of course, about the major issues which you would like to raise concerning that book which we are talking about. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Judge Prandler. As a witness, I wasn't able to express my opinion. I was answering questions. That's the first point. The second point is this: When I studied sociology for four semesters, I listened to lectures from systematic psychology and other psychological courses, and after that I spent time dealing with problems of that kind and that subject matter, and I claim and state that a lack of understanding of social psychology, which -- well, every textbook in the world today explains what the basic forms of behaviour are, and without an understanding of that, you can't understand this case. That is why I am the best-placed person to explain the basic mechanisms of human behaviour in given circumstances, whether it's the war in Iraq, or whether it's when there's a power cut in New York, or whether it's in the van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam [as interpreted], or anything else. So it's the failure to understand human behaviour under extreme circumstances that indictments of this kind are developed. That is why it is necessary to understand the basic scientific premises and understandings of social psychology, and this textbook testifies to that. It is about many experiments performed by many scientists, and I claim that without a knowledge of that kind and without this particular textbook, and without scientific evaluation, it is impossible to understand how the crimes in Mi Lai were committed, how people behaved when they're placed in prison, where we have the role-playing of prisoner and guard by students and so on, how authority functions, how groups function, and so on and so forth, and all that is contained in Professor Sakic's report. Now, I think I am fully capable of asking questions on that subject matter. I am well versed in those problems. I understood them before the war, I understood them during the war. I was head of the department where Mr. Sakic was working in and where there were a large group of sociologists and social psychologists that dealt with the war in Croatia and dealt with all these problems and were trying to translate scientific knowledge into practice, and I think that gives me every possible qualification, all my knowledge and expertise, to raise these questions. If somebody feels that they can answer these questions better than me, I don't mind. I don't mind having the Judges go through all the elements contained in this social psychology book, social contamination and all the other aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would say that it would be better if you start with your questions now than to continue, for minutes and minutes and minutes, with your arguments which we know quite well. So then please proceed, but within the framework which the Chamber has determined many times ago -- and also many times and a long time ago. So please proceed, but within this framework. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, just a correction to the transcript. On page 24, line 13, it was recorded that General Praljak said that, among others, he can explain the Museum of van Gogh in Amsterdam. He didn't say that. He said that he can explain the killing of Theo van Gogh in Holland.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I can ask -- I'm going to adhere to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, tell me, please, did you have this textbook? Were you an editor? Have you read through it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: It is a textbook titled "Social Psychology," written by Elliot Aronson and his associates, Timothy Wilson and Robin Akert. It is the definitive textbook on social psychology today, and Elliot Aronson is among the best-known social psychologists in the world, and for purposes of illustration he received all three awards of the American Psychological Association for his work in social psychology. Now, this textbook -- well, I initiated its translation into Croatian. It was translated by the publishing house, Mate of Zagreb, and I cooperated with them and it was translated by my associates. I would like to make a technical comment here. You said, General, that I worked in the Ministry for Military Psychology [as interpreted], the Department for Military Psychology, and I just wanted to correct that and say what I actually did do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you please open page 253 of the Croatian text. This is where the book speaks about conformism and about the massacre in Mi Lai in Vietnam, where 450 to 500 Vietnamese were killed. Could you tell us, just in one sentence, what is conformism, how does it act, and what the consequences can be if people conform to the group?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's very difficult to say all that in one sentence. I'll try and be as brief as possible. Conformistic behaviour is the most common social behaviour in human groups, and we all conform to a certain implicit or explicit social norms. In order not to expand the matter any further, I would just say that we are interested in the negative aspects of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can wait until the sentence is fully translated, but I just wanted, as I took the floor, to draw the attention regarding the transcript to the fact that this is always "conformism" and not "confirmism," with an O and not an I. The verb is correctly transcribed in page 26, line 25. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The question was this: Can this lead to perilous things, such as, for example, the massacre in Mi Lai?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the positive effects of conformism and social behaviour that we call conformistic behaviour, there are also negative aspects of our conformist behaviour which are most commonly reflected in the so-called information and normative social influence. The negative aspects of information and normative social influence, and some other negative aspects relative to the information and normative social influences, such as social contamination, can lead to crimes such as the crime in Mi Lai and similar crimes. According to the social and psychological insight and the social and psychological logic, this is absolutely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're talking about pages 258, 259, and 260 of the Croatian text. Here, you can see a reference to social contamination. Do you know that the information and social influences can lead to mass disease without any reality, such as the case that took place in the state of Tennessee when --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, and it has often very happened in human history and it still continues to happen. This is a recent event, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to avoid any interruptions and wasting time, when the general mentions pages in the book "Social Psychology," and the number is 3D03521, the pages -- page numbers are the same as in the English text. There are slight discrepancies, but as you can see, the book has been translated in such a way that the illustrations and the appearance of the book has been retained from the English original, which means that the Croatian copy corresponds with the English original.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before you continue, it appears, unless my copy is unique, which is possible - I know there's a lot of copying that goes on - but unless it's -- there appears to be another problem in using this report, because I don't have those pages in the English version. My version skips from page 254 to 260, so I can't follow the testimony of the witness or the references to the book without having the proper page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, there must be a confusion with the numbers because the English pages are only the ones that are being referred to. The general mentioned page numbers 258, 259 and 260, and the pages should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please check?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no page 258, 259, or 255, or 256, or 257, so -- the general just referred to those specific pages, and we can't follow this testimony unless we have the proper material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Trying to assist, do you have figures at the bottom of the page, on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This page, 259, where this mass psychogenic illness is mentioned, is 3D430571.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we must have completely different material.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. You must have -- I'm waiting for the microphone to come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence can give you a functioning copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what happened here. I have the pages in English, 254, 255, 256, 257, 259, 260, and so on and so forth, and I will gladly provide my copy to my learned friend, and I'll take his. If you can bear with me for a couple of minutes, I'll take the pages from my binder. Everything has been copied in an automatic photocopier in the Defence room, and I don't see any reason why the Prosecutor's copy should differ from ours. This has not happened before. It just simply cannot be. I apologise. The Prosecution has made its own copy, and that's -- that may be the root of the problem. But I will gladly provide my copy to my learned friend. If I could ask the usher's assistance with providing my learned friend with my copy of the document. Your Honours, the OTP photocopies its own documents. This document has been in e-court for a long time. They've been provided the numbers. So if my learned friend has not prepared properly, that's not our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There's no reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no reason for these personal comments. No moral blame was indicated. All I simply indicated was I didn't have certain pages, and counsel's -- sorry, I don't want to over react, but it's completely inappropriate. All of a sudden, it's my fault, I haven't prepared properly. My goodness. All I said was I didn't have those pages. If counsel has assisted me, I thank him for that, but it's really not necessary to get personal about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 261, Witness, and tell me in what situations people might conform to the information and social influence.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Most commonly, this happens when people are confronted in ambiguous situations, in crisis situations, and in situations when the source of information which exerts the information and social influence is another person who is an expert or authority in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I asked you this in order to be able to ask you yet another question. The massacre in Mi Lai, was it the consequence of circumstances, or the decision by one or two commanders, or did this decision come from the top echelons of the American Army? What was the cause of such behaviour? Was it a random situation, was it predictable, was it the result of the chain of command? What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I would be inclined to side up with my colleague Aronson who made a sociological analysis, a very extensive one about the case in Mi Lai, and based on a number of arguments, one could confirm that from the social and psychological perspective, no military hierarchy or command was needed for the event to happen in the way it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My second question. In mass psychosis that sometimes appear, would one be able to conclude that based on a fiction or rumours, there can be real damages to a person's health?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: The mass psychogenous disease does relate to bad health without any symptoms. Now that you've mentioned the school in Tennessee, this is an example of an information influence having a major influence. This was the case here because the information came from the teacher in the classroom, and the teacher was treated as an expert or an authority in that case, and thus the effect of that information on the population, and the information was that she could smell gasoline, and that because of the smell of gasoline that she could smell, she could also feel physical symptoms, such as dizziness, headache, faintness, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. Who do you refer to by "she"? Who is she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the teacher in the classroom, which was the origin of the mass psychogenous disease in Tennessee. It is a typical example of the information and sociological influence that caused the spread of the social disease, first in the classroom that she was teaching and then across the school, and everybody fell ill without any organic cause for the illness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 278 now and part of page 279. Will the process to conform be stronger if a group is compact, and how can different cultural and sociological groups influence the strength of the process to conform to that group?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: In my report, you can find a lot of information about the theories of social identity which discuss the phenomenon of the so-called multi-individualistic or -- as opposed to multi-pluralistic cultures. This is the phenomenon that interests sociologists across the world. Collectivist groups will appear more often in collectivist cultures, of course, and the collectivism of those cultures can be caused by various social categories. It can be caused by ideology, by religion, by nationalism, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now let's go -- or, rather, in your book you mention Milgram's research with regard to subordination of authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and in my report I mention all the terms that you are referring to from Aronson's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On pages 288?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question is "in your book." Now, the book is not the witness's book, but he speaks of the Milgram also in his report, and I must confess I do not understand why you put this with regard to a book rather than with regard to his book, where he talks about this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, when I said "in your book," I misspoke. I meant to say "in your report." I misspoke. I can't say "in your book," because obviously this is not his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On pages 288, 289, and 290, and 291 - in your report you have referred to those pages - tell me, please, what are the exact conclusions as a result of Milgram's research within the framework of subordination to the authority of a group?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the description of the experiment, Milgram introduced ordinary people to the experiment - they were normal citizens - and that that experiment, in which he researched the willingness of people to be subjugated to the authority, it showed the extreme proneness of people to be subjugated in certain situations to various authorities. In this particular case, the authority was himself, in his role as a university professor and the leader of the experiment. His conclusion was that this points to the force of the information and social influence, and the negative effects of the information and social influences if they originate from an authority and, of course, if the instructions by the authority and the information that he provides is erroneous and misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: People in -- who used these experiments to inflict such strong shocks, were they normal, ordinary people, bureaucrats, students, citizens?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a sample of a civic population in America, and I must say that this is a series of experiments which are the best-known experiments in social psychology which were conducted in all cultures, not only in America, and the results were interpreted and confirmed in other cultures in the same or similar ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your report, you mentioned one more thing, the system of the social role and its power. So now on page 302 and 303 of the textbook -- well, those are the pages you'll find that reference on, and tell the Trial Chamber about these experiments in Stanford, Banks and Zimbardo conducting them, how people behaved to whom certain roles are assigned, whether they're normal people, whether the group was a group of citizens, a random selection of individuals. So just explain it to us briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: It was a population of students from Stanford University, and they knew that in the basement of their university a prison had been set up, an artificial prison, of course, they knew it wasn't a real one, and they knew that their roles were assigned randomly by a throw of the dice. Now, those who were supposed to play the role of the prisoners, they were dressed in prisoner garb. They had a chain and a lock on their leg, and they had a nylon cap on their head, rubber slippers or shoes. Now, the guards had a yellow uniform; that is to say, they were dressed differently. And they wanted to conduct this expert over a fortnight, but they had to interrupt it after only six days because there was -- what happened was extreme identification both of the prisoners and the guards on their roles. The prisoners became helpless, and the guards launched verbal abuse and very creative in their -- in thinking up verbal abuse, and they behaved very sadistically towards the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, in that expert did anybody intervene on the side of the guards to influence them in their behaviour or was their behaviour spontaneous because of this spontaneous social role or, rather, the well-defined social roles they were supposed to play?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: No, the expert implied that nobody would interfere. The people conducting the experiment were just the observers, and when they saw that things had gone too far and could have adverse repercussions, they interrupted the experiment, stopped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Now, this experiment was repeated many times and similar results were always obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, you also mention individuation and de-individuation and the loss of people in a group; 321, 323 are the pages numbers. So tell us what actually happens when you put people into a uniform, when you put them into a large group? Lynchings are mentioned, and they were examined. So, tell us, what people -- what are people capable of doing when they can hide behind a mass and when that mass is depicted by a uniform or whatever, by the clothes they wear? What happens?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: For de-individuation to take place, we have to mention that before that, there must be a firm cohesion in a group, where individuals are prone to de-individuation, and then you have collective behaviour, collective behaviour is the behaviour of a certain group faced in spontaneous -- faced with spontaneous situations, and that this -- what happens in war very frequently, spontaneous situations in which the group complies with hastily-designed rules, and then you have these rules affecting the social norms of a group. In extreme behaviour of this kind, the extremist collective behaviour, in which each attack on the group is felt by the individuals of that group as being an attack against an individual, and what happens is extreme instances of de-individuation, in which, to simplify terms, the individual melts into the whole, he loses the normal restrictions that he would have in behaviour, limitations, and then is ready, given that type of situation, to engage in deviant and impulsive behaviour, including the most extremist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, in groups of this kind, does the aggressiveness of individuals increase because the individual has been immersed into this group and de-individualised in the mass?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Aggressiveness in that group is justified, and one type of aggressive behaviour leads to another type of aggressive behaviour. They feed each other. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time for a break, and I'd like to have a break, please, if I may. I'm a little tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Let me first read an oral decision, oral decision on how Witness Dragan Curcic is to be examined. Witness Dragan Curcic must testify before the Trial Chamber under Rule 92 ter on October 12 and 13, 2009. In a letter of September 29, 2009, the Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to be allowed to have two hours for its cross-examination. During the hearing of September 30th, 2009, the Prosecution made its -- renewed its request, whereas the Petkovic Defence made an oral submission to the Trial Chamber on the same day, in order to be granted leave to cross-examine witness Dragan Curcic for 45 to 60 minutes. The Trial Chamber notes that according to the latest updated schedule of the Praljak Defence witnesses sent today, the examination-in-chief of Witness Dragan Curcic will be an hour long. Given the topics addressed by the witness in his written statement, the Trial Chamber decides to grant leave --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To grant, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Prosecution's request and to give it two hours for its cross-examination. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber decides to allocate one hour and thirty minutes to all Defence teams for their cross-examination, and invites the Defence teams to distribute this time allocated among themselves. The Trial Chamber believes that given the time allocated to all Defence teams, and given that no specific request was made by the other Defence teams, that the Petkovic Defence should have enough time for its cross-examination, without requiring any additional time. As a consequence, the Trial Chamber rejects the time for additional time made by the Petkovic Defence. In a word, the Praljak Defence will have one hour, the Prosecution will have two hours, and all other Defence teams will have an hour and thirty minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to inform you -- well, thank you for that decision. Everything is clear. I'd just like to tell you that with respect to the Curcic distribution time, the Defence needs one hour, and that is a maximum -- the maximum time. So during the preparations, we find that it might be considerably less than an hour. So I just wanted to inform you of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question concerning the topics that you addressed earlier. You talked about the Milgram experiment, and a French movie was actually made out of this experiment. It was called "I comme icare," and the lead actor was Yves Montand. So everyone knows about the Milgram experiment. It was carried out in several countries, and it demonstrates that about 70 per cent of people obey authority, whatever orders are given by the authority. Do you agree with this percentage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to Milgram's experiment, well, that is roughly the percentage according to which those examined use a maximum shock of 450 volts, which inflict on the person -- well, the experiment referred -- looked at how punishment affected learning and memory. Now, you're talking about an analogous application of those results now, which would, in fact, mean that about 70 per cent of people were ready to become subjugated to the orders of an authority according to the principles of spontaneous conformism, and the very fact that the authority and behaviour of an authority is socially permissible. Let me just add -- well, you're talking about the film. However, the experiment was also done on German television in 1980 publicly, and it gave the same results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor Sakic, Judge Antonetti asked you about a subjugation [realtime transcript read in error "subrogation"] to authority, so are we talking about the structure of society or subjugation to an authority within a group? Which?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about subjugation to the phenomenon of authority. Authority can be a broad concept. It can be any person who, in a given situation, has the best solutions for the group. That is what we mean by authority within the group. Now, power, for example -- authority in the context of power under a state is the president of a state or the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. But these people are citizens, and as citizens they knew that the torture of others is not an acceptable form of social behaviour, in none of the countries in which the experiment was conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: That is correct, and that is precisely why people, during these experiments, had a great deal of psychological problems and impressive reactions, but they did not give up on the various levels of shock. So that's what's interesting in that particular experiment. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just propose a change to the transcript. On page 39, line 10, the word "subrogation" to an authority is used, and also on two lines further up. I think that the word is "subjugation," "submission." Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, what I've been asking you about, everything we've been discussing, is it incorporated as knowledge in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are basic theoretical concepts which I used in my report. However, I used a much broader context as well, a broader theoretical context, taken from this book and from other books, as you can see from the listed references.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's take a look at page 314 and 315, parts of 317, 18, 19, 20, and 21, where group decisions are discussed, so whether one head is better than two, whether there is a blindness, polarisation towards extremes, or what I call the radicalisation of the group towards the most radical of its members. So could you link all this up with a theory of cultural values which, of course, must also be introduced into any social and psychological study because there are, of course, cultures -- differences between cultures and civilisations? So, just briefly, what you can tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: What we're dealing here -- what we're dealing with here is how decisions are made in a group. Today, the civilised world, at different levels and in different systems, makes decisions usually in groups, it is a group decision, because the realisation was reached that if a group follows a certain scenario in making its decisions, then the decisions will be better taken by the group than by an individual. Now, what you're talking about is the negative aspect of decision-making within groups, and there are several phenomena there; the phenomenon of losses within the process and then the phenomenon of group blindness which is based on the theory of the group. The author is Bibla Tanaj [phoen], an American psychology, that talks about this group blindness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to give a more extensive explanation? It would require some time. Anyway, these losses in the process occur when a group does not take on board all the arguments, but makes its decisions exclusively on the basis of information on which all the members of the group agree, and decisions like that usually have negative consequences. Now, group blindness is a more serious phenomenon, and the problem occurs there because a decision is made in highly-cohesive groups which have their guiding light -- guiding leader, the person who does not discuss matters on the basis of information relevant to a decision, but guides the group in conformity with his own opinions and positions. Then there are bad methods in that, and, finally, while the group is making its decisions, is isolated. So the symptoms of group blindness exist on many counts; illusions of invulnerability, the supremacy of a group, or they think that they are -- have a position of supremacy towards others, and then there is auto-censorship within the group, and then people who think differently are made to keep silent. And then there are guardians of opinions, those who guard the others to see that they follow the thinking of the leader. So the decisions are partial, they don't take into account any risk factor, they don't use broad sources of information and data, and ultimately they have no alternative if they prove unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: You said something about culture and civilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave cultural aspects.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to go on about the risks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll skip that. A war is a conflict. Now, could you tell us about what you've written? Well, look at 325 -- page 325, 326, and could you tell us what the elements of a conflict and what elements of cooperation are, either on a theoretical level or practically, as we're going to see later on? The pages are 325 and 326. Go ahead, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in this context of conflict and cooperation, basic questions have to be asked, that is to say, in what way the individuals who are in conflict can be brought to cooperate or how to resolve the conflict, and this analyses the many dilemmas, one of them being the social dilemma, and the most useful procedure for the individual, if he is elected by the group, becomes detrimental to the whole group. Another important aspect of this same question is the following: The attempt to resolve the conflict through threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to expound?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you've written about that in your report, threats as a means of resolving conflicts. But in the USA, why are there more killings than in other countries, comparing the figures to Canada, for example?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, there are many interpretations of this, but most frequently it is because of the presence of large quantities of arms in America, lots of weapons that you can carry legally, and a lot of illegal weapons, too, for that matter, so that social psychology and aggressive behaviour -- well, the presence of weapons, as Leonid Berkovich said, this is an aggressive sign, in the theoretical sense, and therefore it can give rise to additional aggression with the ordinary man. And so because of the many weapons that people have in the American society, the consequences will be greater linked to the higher rates of killings, compared to Canada, where it is illegal to carry arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now look at page 329, please, and the application of threats in the resolution of conflicts and how people behave. And you have there that famous Deutsch and Krauss experiments, so could you explain that to Their Honours? I think you mention it in your expert report.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It would require a little time, so do you want just the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, this expert showed -- they're classical experiments conducted by two psychologists, Deutsch and Krauss in the 1960s, and they showed that threats -- well, what they wanted to see was whether threats could be used to resolve a conflict between two sides, as threats are very often present in our daily lives. A mother, for example, tries to threaten her child, or in school, or whatever, to regulate behaviour. But in this experiment, we found that a threat, not only does it not establish cooperation among the two sides, but the greater the threat, the greater the conflict between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it then true that when threats become realistic before the outbreak of a war, for example, that there is a greater probability that the conflict will flare up, unless there are any factors to act against this, rather than finding peaceful solutions, not only in war, the war in the former Yugoslavia, but any conflict or war, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: In keeping with that experiment, threats never achieve the desired effect. Other measures are called for in case of war and in the case that you mentioned, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move on to a very important section that people have been dealing with from time immemorial, and that's the question of aggression dealt with here on page 417, 418, 19, and onwards. So, please, what are the -- what is aggression? Is it nature or nurture?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Aggression is hostile behaviour towards another person, with the aim of inflicting psychological or physical pain. There are two basic types of aggression, hostile aggression and instrumental aggression. Hostile aggression aims at inflicting pain, it has no other aim, whereas instrumental aggression does not have the aim of primarily inflicting pain, but there is another objective, another aim; for example, to loot. And that is why war can be considered to be the most widespread form of instrumental aggression, because basically a war, according to Erich Fromm, always has a rational goal; that is to say, to use aggression to achieve another goal. It is not violence -- it is not just violence and the killing of people, of itself. Now, there are biological and social elements linked to aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One more question with this regard. Within the understanding of Erich Fromm, when he speaks about war as instrumental aggression, does this also comprise hostile aggression, and to what extent does hostile aggression, within the instrumental aggression, influence the duration of a war, its development, its spiralling, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I've already explained that in my report. Fromm's thesis has been widely accepted nowadays with regard to explaining the causes of war. He claims that war is caused by irrational instincts in a human being. This is a thesis that is unacceptable, he says. He says that from Greek -- ancient Greek times to modern times, every war has had rational goals and objectives, be it economical goods, territories, and so on and so forth. Very well, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 419 --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: I meant to explain the appearance of the other type, how does war appear. War is a new context for a psychological -- sociological psychologist, and within that new context not every rule applies, those rules that a war starts with, and within that new context there can also be hostile acts of aggression, not only instrumental aggression but also hostile aggression that are aimed at inflicting pain, and that has been happening in every war so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 419, and you have also dealt with the problem of aggression in different cultures, here reference is made to the West European civilisation circle that we belong to. Then there is a reference to oligarchy, aggression, the culture of honour, and so on and so forth. Could you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: In the book, the phenomenon has not been paid much attention. The phenomena has otherwise been a very widely studied, and it is a subject of many -- it has been the subject of many studies within the disciplines of anthropology, social psychology, and sociology. It should be noted here that an American circle of anthropologists has dealt with this topic very intensely from the 30s to 50s of last century. Among them were Margaret Mead and Ruth Benedict as its most prominent representatives. And it should also be noted that President Roosevelt contacted Ruth Benedict during the war and he contacted her group as well in order to explain the phenomena of different propensity to aggression in different culture, and especially with regard to the then American enemies, Germans and Japanese.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor Sakic --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: So it is a common standpoint shared by anthropologists, sociologists, and social psychologists that not all cultures are equally prone to aggression. In other words, there are societies which have, within their system of values, an increased propensity towards aggressive behaviour. Fromm speaks about that in his book, "The Anatomy of Human Destructivity."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And now, Professor, a question that goes beyond this context. In the Second World War, do you know how many American psychologists worked for the American military, especially when it came to establishing positive selection, and how many interviews and other investigations they carried out in order to select higher officers and officers? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC
utterances.text: Of course. America has actually introduced psychology and psychologists into the discipline of war. The most -- the best-known case prior to the Second World War is Woodworth's series alpha and beta intelligence tests. Those tests were used to test American soldiers or, rather, those who applied that they wanted to go to Europe to war, and they were subject to those tests.
